posts.name: Unsafe_Bet
posts.cooked:
Matchstickman:

>G needed a term and chose Indestructible, then they defined it in the rulebook, it's what it means for this game, I would not walk into a game of HeroClix and expect Indestructible to mean the same thing there as here.

I expect the word to mean what the word means.  If you created a game and used the term "card" in that game to refer to a six-sided object which is rolled to produce random numbers, I'd call that bad game design.  The English language (or any other) is a tool which can be used correctly or incorrectly in the pursuit of any project.  Giving a misleading name to an important piece of rules text was an unfortunate decision, one of the relatively few mistakes that >G made in creating this mostly-excellent game, which I'd correct if given the chance to create a still-better version.

Because? People who come across a term they haven't encountered before in a game tend to reach for the rules to see what it means, rather than guessing.

Nonsense.  When a word's meaning seems obvious, they have no reason to second-guess the assumption and check a rulebook, particularly not when playing a game with such simplistic rules (and built-in teamwork, ensuring that only one player really needs to know the details of how it functions) as SOTM, where a rulebook is barely even necessary, and a glossary is easily overlooked until you have to look up a term whose meaning doesn't seem obvious.  I'd never even look at a word whose meaning I figured I already knew, because why assume that the game pointlessly revises the meanings of common-enough English words?  If Into the Stratosphere didn't say "non-indestructible", there'd be every reason to assume that it works on a Galvanize or an Advanced Matriarch's Cohort, if that was the first indestructible card you encountered.  Tempest's player would be annoyed if he played this differently-written ItS, only to have you rebuke him with some highly counterintuitive wording from the rulebook.

And Indestructible works better thematically, and I'm pretty sure that's a high priority in the way >G create games.

That's the closest part of your argument to validity, but I still think it's not the best choice, though it might be a reasonably decent one.  "Can't leave play" or "unremovable" or "permanent" would all work better IMO.

posts.name: Pydro
posts.cooked:
"Indestructible" might not be the perfect word, but it is the best word. 99.9% of the time when a card leaves play it is because it is destroyed. If you want to have a word that prevents that, having the perfect antonym would be the most intutive decision. Is it the clearest for all situations? Maybe not, but for 99.9% of the time it is clearer than any other word. Let's say it did say "Can't leave play," there would be many questions asking "How does a card leave play without being destroyed?" Which is better, to have a question each time the word came up, or have a question the rare times that an exception comes up.

Regardless, you have yet to give a good alternative to "indestructible." Everything you gave will lead to many more questions. For example, the card doesn't leave play, but was it destroyed to trigger "on destruction" effects? The way SotM is setup, this question is wide open, but by having the word indestructible, the question is completely eliminated.

However, there will be other specific cases. For example, if it said cannot leave play, how does it interact with Savage Mana? The card is still in play, so would Savage Mana work or not?

Essentially, it comes down to the following: if you can't have a perfect word, you want the most intuitive word, which would be the perfect antonym to the situation that comes up 99.9% of the time.

I also want to add that the argument of "I shouldn't have to read the rulebook" is ridiculous.

posts.cooked:
Powerhound_2000:

I'm not sure I understand your argument at all Unsafe_Bet.  Into the Stratosphere is the only card that could potentially remove an Indestructible card from play but it says on the card itself that it can't be used on Indestructible cards. 

Is it really the only one that exists as of yet?  I thought for certain I'd noticed others.  At the very least, it limits the options for future design.  "Temporarily remove a thing from play while knowing that it will come back" is a nice piece of technology for card games to have access to.

Pydro:

99.9% of the time when a card leaves play it is because it is destroyed. If you want to have a word that prevents that, having the perfect antonym would be the most intutive decision.

Why not 100%?  You should always keep your eyes on the outliers, since they are what requires such attention.  Obvious answers are easily produced.

Let's say it did say "Can't leave play," there would be many questions asking "How does a card leave play without being destroyed?" Which is better, to have a question each time the word came up, or have a question the rare times that an exception comes up.

Actually now that I think about it, that one may not be a great suggestion, since it might give some folks the idea that the card still counts as "destroyed" even though it doesn't leave play.  However I don't know how many people would think to ask your question.

I also want to add that the argument of "I shouldn't have to read the rulebook" is ridiculous.

Considering that the rulebook is like eight pages and three of them are just character bios, and the whole thing is in large print, not having much need to read what little they did print, since someone else can just explain it to you, seems eminently reasonable.  There's no reason there should be anything hidden away in the rules which you'd always need to know but would never think to go looking for.  The purpose of a rulebook is to enable you to look up answers when a question occurs to you, and "can I not-destroy this indestructible card" is not a question many people would think to ask.

Silverleaf:

Isn't this a bit moot? What do you want G+ to do about it, make up a new word and replace everyone's games?

They could issue errata and correct future printings.  I'm not even saying I want them to, just that the option exists.  We already have to mentally rewrite the rules on the cards in the case of old copies of Solar Flare etc. (since the replacement cards are the wrong size and can't actually replace them).  For that matter, they could print replacement cards again, if this ever became a large enough issue to require such measures.
